screens.title: Storing Simple Data with Shared Preferences
screens.subtitle: Lightweight local persistence for settings and small state

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn when a key-value store is the right choice and how to use the shared_preferences plugin to persist small bits of app state. Shared preferences are best for things like user settings, a 'remember me' flag, UI state, or the last known selection — data that must survive app restarts but does not require a full database. You'll see how to add the dependency, acquire the shared preferences instance, write and read primitive types, and avoid common asynchronous mistakes. I'll show a concrete counter example that persists a number, and a typical settings pattern that saves a theme flag and username. We'll also cover naming conventions for keys and why you should avoid storing secrets here. By the end you'll understand the plugin's limits, how to avoid race conditions by awaiting operations, and how to choose keys so different features don't overwrite each other. Consider how this lightweight persistence improves user experience by restoring state immediately after launch. Ready to explore the concrete topics and the sample code walkthrough that follow?

keyIdea.title: When to use shared_preferences
keyIdea.text: Use it for non-sensitive, small key-value data like settings, simple state, and UI flags — not for secure or complex data.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to choose when shared preferences are the right tool, integrate the plugin into a Flutter project, and read and write the basic primitive types safely. You'll also learn to manage asynchronous calls so your UI remains responsive and to design stable key names to avoid accidental overwrites. Finally, you'll practice a concrete pattern: load preferences during widget initialization, update them on user interaction, and provide sensible defaults if a key is missing. These skills matter because many mobile apps rely on fast local persistence for user settings and session details. A concrete example is saving a user's chosen theme so the app appears in the preferred mode immediately after launch. Another is persisting a small counter or last-viewed tab so users resume where they left off. You'll also recognize the limitations: this approach is not secure encryption and should not be used for passwords or secrets. Practice these objectives in the hands-on activity and the counter code walkthrough to gain confidence and avoid common mistakes.

screens.title: What shared_preferences is and when to use it
screens.subtitle: A definition and practical use cases

narration.text: Shared preferences is a cross-platform Flutter plugin that provides a simple key-value store backed by platform storage — user defaults on Apple platforms and shared preferences on Android. The key idea is simplicity: you store primitives by key and retrieve them later. This is not a database; it is best for small configuration values, feature flags, UI state like the last selected tab, and user preferences such as a display name or theme choice. For example, saving a boolean named isDarkMode allows your app to apply the correct theme at startup without querying a server. A common misconception is that this provides security — it does not. Do not store passwords or A P I keys here. Another subtle point is that the plugin operates asynchronously: acquiring the singleton preferences instance and writing values both return Futures that should be awaited. If you plan to cache many complex objects or large lists, prefer a database or a file-based solution. Key takeaway: shared preferences is the right tool when you need fast, local, low-volume persistence to restore UX state quickly. screens.title: Add and initialize shared_preferences
screens.subtitle: Dependency, import, and obtaining the instance

narration.text: Start by adding shared_preferences as a dependency in your pubspec file and fetching packages. Once imported, the pattern centers on obtaining a singleton instance and always awaiting that call. In practice this looks like calling the getInstance method on SharedPreferences inside an async context or initState of a stateful widget. If you fail to await the instance, you'll likely encounter null object errors because the prefs object isn't ready yet. The typical flow is: declare a variable to hold the preferences, call getInstance and await it, then read initial values and call setState to apply them to the UI. When writing, call the appropriate set method and await it if subsequent logic depends on the save completing. A small but important detail is where you call getInstance — initState is a good place because it runs early, but remember to perform async work safely by defining an async helper called from initState. This prevents blocking the UI thread while making sure your values are available when the widget renders. As you code, test the startup path and deliberately simulate delays to ensure your UI handles the asynchronous retrieval gracefully.

screens.title: Counter app walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Load and persist an integer across restarts

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete counter example that persists its value with shared preferences. The pattern has three parts: load on startup, update state on increment, and save after changes. On startup, call getInstance and await it, then read the integer by its key and provide a default of zero if missing. When the user increments the counter, update the in-memory state and then call the setInt method to persist the new value. If you forget to await setInt and you immediately read back the value, you can encounter a race where the read happens before the write completes. Another common pattern in the example is using a late variable to hold the preferences instance after initialization so subsequent writes reuse it. In practice, ensure your init helper sets that late variable before any UI callback attempts to write. The code shown in the visual panel is a full example you can paste into a Flutter app; focus on where getInstance is awaited in the load helper and where setInt is awaited after increments. After reviewing the code, try closing and reopening your app to confirm the count persists as expected. What might you change to make this pattern reusable across multiple widgets?

keyIdea.title: Load → Update → Save
keyIdea.text: Load saved value in init, update state on user action, and persist with set methods (await writes when order matters).

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Counter Walkthrough
Core pattern
  1. Obtain and await the preferences instance in an async init helper.
  2. Read the saved int or use a default if null.
  3. On increment, update state and call setInt, awaiting if next actions depend on completion.
Analogy
Treat the device store like a small notebook: write updates you want to survive restarts and read them at the next launch.
Example code
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Persistent Counter',
      home: const MyHomePage(),
    );
  }
}

class MyHomePage extends StatefulWidget {
  const MyHomePage({super.key});

  @override
  State createState() => _MyHomePageState();
}

class _MyHomePageState extends State {
  int _counter = 0;
  late SharedPreferences _prefs; // Will be initialized

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _loadCounter();
  }

  Future<void> _loadCounter() async {
    _prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
    setState(() {
      _counter = _prefs.getInt('counter') ?? 0;
    });
  }

  Future<void> _incrementCounter() async {
    setState(() {
      _counter++;
    });
    await _prefs.setInt('counter', _counter);
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      body: Center(
        child: Text('Count: $_counter', style: const TextStyle(fontSize: 24)),
      ),
      floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(
        onPressed: _incrementCounter,
        child: const Icon(Icons.add),
      ),
    );
  }
}
Tip: place the load helper in initState so UI starts with persisted values when ready.

screens.title: Read and write methods for primitive types
screens.subtitle: Which set / get method to use and default handling

narration.text: The shared_preferences A P I exposes typed set and get methods for each primitive: setBool/getBool, setInt/getInt, setDouble/getDouble, setString/getString, and setStringList/getStringList. Use the matching pair for predictable behavior. When you read a value, the get method may return null if the key doesn't exist, so always provide a sensible default or null-check the result. For example, when loading a theme flag you might assign the value or default to false if null. For lists of strings, prefer setStringList rather than serializing a list into a single string; the dedicated method preserves structure and avoids parsing errors. A common misconception is that get methods always return a non-null value — they don't. Another pitfall is using the wrong setter for the stored data type; writing an int with setString can create confusion and runtime surprises when reading. Finally, remember writes often return a Future that completes when the platform finishes the operation. If you need to guarantee that a value has been stored before proceeding, await the set call. This guarantees deterministic behavior and avoids race conditions in read-after-write scenarios. Read and write methods for primitive types means always use the typed set/get methods and handle nulls by providing defaults; prefer setstringlist for string lists.. In practical terms, which set / get method to use and default handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Asynchronous pitfalls and race conditions
screens.subtitle: Why awaiting matters and how to avoid timing bugs

narration.text: A frequent source of bugs is misunderstanding the asynchronous nature of shared preferences operations. Both obtaining the instance and the write methods return Futures, so failing to await them can create race conditions. For example, if your save method starts a setBool without awaiting and you immediately call a load function, the load might run before the write completes and return an old value. Another mistake is calling getInstance in multiple places and not reusing the same stored instance, which can lead to inconsistent behavior or redundant initialization. Using a late variable assigned after the awaited getInstance call and reusing that variable for writes reduces overhead and avoids timing issues. Also, avoid performing heavy synchronous work on initState; instead use an async helper and setState after the awaited calls complete. Finally, be aware that set methods typically return a boolean success indicator — awaiting them gives you the chance to react to failure. By treating these operations as asynchronous and designing flows that await critical steps, you prevent confusing bugs and ensure predictable persistence behavior. Asynchronous pitfalls and race conditions means always await getinstance and writes when subsequent logic depends on completed persistence to avoid race conditions.. screens.title: Key naming, defaults, and security considerations
screens.subtitle: Design choices that prevent bugs and protect users

narration.text: Designing keys and handling sensitive data are both important when using shared preferences. Adopt a consistent naming scheme: prefix keys with the feature or domain name, such as settings_isDarkMode or user_lastLoginTime. This minimizes accidental collisions when different parts of the app write similar names. Always supply defaults or handle nulls gracefully when reading keys; for example, default booleans to false and strings to a friendly 'Guest'. For lists of tags, use setStringList to preserve structure. Regarding security, shared preferences is not an encrypted store. Do not persist passwords, A P I secrets, or personal financial data here. If you must store sensitive information, choose a secure storage solution that uses platform keychains or encryption. Finally, consider developer ergonomics: centralize preference keys and accessors in a small utility class so changes in naming or migration strategies are easier to maintain. These practices improve reliability, reduce bugs, and make future migrations straightforward. Key naming, defaults, and security considerations means use descriptive keys, handle defaults, centralize access, and avoid storing sensitive data in shared preferences.. screens.title: Common assessment questions and how to answer them
screens.subtitle: Example quiz items and explanations

narration.text: Two assessment items capture common knowledge checks. First, when asked which method to use to store a list of user-selected tags, the correct answer is the string-list setter because shared preferences provides a dedicated setStringList method that preserves the list structure without manual serialization. Choosing a single concatenated string is possible but adds parsing complexity and potential errors. Second, when save and load functions run back-to-back, a likely issue is a race condition caused by not awaiting the save operation. The fix is to make the save function async and await the set call before loading. During troubleshooting, look for missing awaits, misuse of the wrong typed setter, or inconsistent key names. If a value is unexpectedly null on load, verify the key spelling and that the write completed successfully. These assessment-style checks reinforce the importance of typed methods, awaiting asynchronous operations, and consistent key naming — the design patterns that make shared preferences reliable in production apps. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, shared preferences is a lightweight key-value store ideal for non-sensitive primitives and small lists. Second, the A P I is asynchronous: you must await instance retrieval and writes when the order of operations matters. Third, use typed set and get methods and handle null results by supplying defaults. Fourth, adopt clear key naming to avoid collisions and centralize access for maintainability. Fifth, never store highly sensitive information here; use secure storage solutions for secrets. These principles will help you design predictable, user-friendly persistence for settings and small state in your Flutter apps. As you build the counter and the settings screen, focus on awaiting critical operations, reusing the preferences instance, and testing startup behavior after app restarts.
